subject: Tiger-Woods
research_tasks: Before drafting quotes, open the ASAP Sports Hall of Fame transcript (S14) or the speech video directly. Confirm the wording of the 'earn it ... That defined my career' passage, and whether 'instilled in me this work ethic' refers to his father, his mother or both (Golf Channel vs the PGA Tour's 2025 obituary).

Verify Gary Smith's 'The Chosen One' quotes (Earl's prophecy; Tiger's 'This is my purpose. It will unfold.'; the Buddhism line) against the SI original or an authorized reprint (S55). The opened copy (S56) is an unauthorized blog reproduction.

Do not use the circulating 1997-book lines 'the control I craved' or 'addicted to staying on the range', Kultida's 'go for the throat ... kill them' (S67), Harmon's 'win by 10', or 'Second sucks' unless an opened source confirms them. Do not attribute Nike's 'Winning takes care of everything' to Woods (S34).
Open a primary report of Greg Norman's LIV offer claim (Washington Post 2022) before using C11. Otherwise drop it or attribute it explicitly as Norman's unconfirmed claim.

Pin the 2026 plea terms from court records or a second wire (ABC says no contest, CBS says guilty; S53/S54) and the date of the 2025 disc-replacement surgery (S45, October 10 vs 'September'). Write 'plea deal on reduced charges' if this cannot be resolved.
Open the original Golf Digest November 2021 interview (S69) or the video to confirm the 'never full time' and Everest quotes, and the Dec 11, 2009 'indefinite break' statement (S04) if it is used.
Check the Rinaldi 2010 wording ('living a life of a lie' vs 'living a lie') against the ESPN video before quoting (S05).

Sensitive-claims handling for the draft: never state a diagnosis (his 2010 statement names only 'the issues I'm facing'). Present the Enquirer deal as reported and later sworn testimony, without naming the photographed woman unless necessary. Present the Herman matter (C33) as allegations later disavowed, or omit it. Frame the 2017 and 2026 arrests as medical and legal facts with dates, not character evidence. Attribute Uchitel's psychological claims (C15) to her.

Optional strengthening for the 8 vs 3 discriminator: find Woods' own words, not testimony, on why he pursued SEAL training, and any interview where he discusses how he felt about his public persona versus his private self.

sources.title: Tiger Woods' apology: Full transcript
sources.speaker: Tiger Woods (prepared statement at TPC Sawgrass), transcript via CNN
sources.locator: Full transcript, opened and read end to end. Key passages: opening ('always tried to be a private person'); infidelity/entitlement paragraph; 'it's not what you achieve in life that matters'; role-model apology; 45 days inpatient therapy; privacy/children paragraph; Buddhism paragraph; return-to-golf paragraph; closing ask.
sources.excerpt: I want to say to each of you, simply, and directly, I am deeply sorry for my irresponsible and selfish behavior I engaged in. / And while I have always tried to be a private person, there are some things I want to say. / My behavior has caused considerable worry to my business partners. / I was unfaithful. I had affairs. I cheated. What I did is not acceptable. And I am the only person to blame. I stopped living by the core values that I was taught to believe in. I knew my actions were wrong. But I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply. I never thought about who I was hurting. Instead, I thought only about myself. I ran straight through the boundaries that a married couple should live by. I thought I could get away with whatever I wanted to. I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled. Thanks to money and fame, I didn't have far -- didn't have to go far to find them. I was wrong. I was foolish. I don't get to play by different rules. / I once heard -- and I believe it is true -- it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome. Achievements on the golf course are only part of setting an example. Character and decency are what really count. Parents used to point to me as a role model for their kids. I owe all of those families a special apology. / For 45 days, from the end of December to early February, I was in inpatient therapy, receiving guidance for the issues I'm facing. / I have always tried to maintain a private space for my wife and children. They have been kept separate from my sponsors, my commercial endorsements / Buddhism teaches that a craving for things outside ourselves causes an unhappy and pointless search for security. It teaches me to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint. Obviously, I lost track of what I was taught. / When I do return, I need to make my behavior more respectful of the game. / I ask you to find room in your hearts to one day believe in me again.
sources.context: A scripted, televised statement read to an invited room of friends, staff, sponsors' representatives and pool reporters, with no questions taken. Delivered 84 days after the 2009-11-27 crash outside his home and 79 days after his 2009-12-02 written statement that problems 'shouldn't have to mean public confessions' (S03). The statement was a public-relations event as well as a confession; its self-analysis uses therapy vocabulary. It names no diagnosis: 'the issues I'm facing' is the only treatment language, so any 'sex addiction' label is not established by his words. The Globe and Mail transcript (S02) matches this wording; AJC's live-typed copy is rougher and should not be quoted.

sources.title: Ten years later: players, caddies and observers marvel at Tiger's 2008 U.S. Open win
sources.speaker: Bob Harig (ESPN), oral history quoting Hank Haney, Steve Williams, Rocco Mediate and Tiger Woods
sources.locator: Haney MRI paragraph; Williams paragraph; Tiger's look-back paragraph
sources.excerpt: Haney: He's explaining about the MRI, it's on his laptop and he's showing there are two stress fractures, as well as the torn ACL. He's showing us everything, but Tiger is not really listening. ... Tiger looks up and says, 'I'm playing the U.S. Open and I'm going to win.' Just like that. Then he says, 'C'mon Hank, let's go practice.' / Williams: I think I asked him on three separate occasions if it was the right thing to carry on. And I got the same reply each time: 'F--- you, Stevie, I'm winning this tournament.' / Tiger: in those four majors, I honestly don't remember missing a putt inside 10 feet.
sources.context: Oral history ten years after the event. Haney and Williams both later fell out with Woods and wrote books, but here they are admiring rather than critical. Medical facts (torn ACL, two tibial stress fractures, doctors' advice of crutches then rest) are reported widely; Woods himself said on his website after winning that 'the right thing to do is to listen to my doctors' (search snippet only).

Later that season Golf Channel's Brandel Chamblee gave him an 'F' for being 'cavalier with the rules', Woods' agent Mark Steinberg threatened action, and Chamblee apologized (search results only; not opened).

sources.title: Emotional, unscripted Tiger Woods focuses on family, upbringing in HOF speech
sources.speaker: Ryan Lavner (Golf Channel), quoting Tiger Woods' World Golf Hall of Fame induction speech
sources.locator: Body (opened via direct download): 'One of the most guarded athletes' paragraph; speech quotes on parents and earning
sources.excerpt: Lavner: He was slated to talk for seven minutes. But he spoke for nearly 17, without notes or the use of a teleprompter. One of the most guarded athletes in history, here now he was speaking from the heart. / Woods: So without the sacrifices of Mom, who took me to all those junior golf tournaments, and Dad, who's not here, but who instilled in me this work ethic to fight for what I believe in, to chase after my dreams - that nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned. If you don't go out there and put in the work, if you don't go out and put in the effort - one, you're not going to get the results, and two, and more importantly, you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. So that defined my upbringing. That defined my career. / Lavner: For 17 unscripted minutes, Woods made only one passing mention of his life and career this century. Nothing about the Tiger Slam. Nothing about the majors. Nothing about the soaring highs. The scandals.
sources.context: Delivered a year after the 2021 crash, before his return to competition. Lavner's account includes Woods hiding in 'The Ditch' at the Navy Golf Course, being denied clubhouse access as a junior because of his skin color, and the family's second mortgage, which he paid off with his first Titleist deal. Celebratory setting; memory is 40 years old. The PGA Tour's 2025 obituary attributes 'instilled in me this work ethic' to his mother; Golf Channel's rendering ties it to 'Dad'. Check the video before assigning it to one parent.

sources.title: The Secret History of Tiger Woods
sources.speaker: Wright Thompson (ESPN The Magazine), with named witnesses (John Brown, Ryan Zinke, Billy Helmers, Joe Grohman, Paul Fregia, Michael Jordan) and unnamed friends
sources.locator: Act I: Earl's death and burial; childhood at the Navy Golf Course. Act II: Fort Bragg 2004, SEAL facility 2006, birthday skydive 2006-12-30, Michael Jordan passage, introvert/marketability passage, Halloween text, 'impersonation' and '30 seconds' narration
sources.excerpt: Narration: Seventy-seven minutes after touching down in Kansas, Tiger took off again for Orange County. / Narration: TWENTY-FIVE DAYS after he buried his father and 15 before the 2006 U.S. Open, Tiger went back to visit the Navy SEALs / Brown: 'Why are you here?' ... 'My dad,' Tiger said, explaining that Earl had told him he'd either end up being a golfer or a special operations soldier. / Brown: I definitely think he was searching for something. / Narration: He chose to spend Dec. 30, 2006 -- his 31st birthday -- in San Diego skydiving with SEALs. / Unnamed friend: Frankly, the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book. / Unnamed friend: Tiger was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality. / Woods (text to Notah Begay about a Halloween costume): I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods. / Narration: Talk to enough people who've met him and it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be. / Narration: People who meet him for 30 seconds love him, and people who spend several hours with him think he's aloof and weird, while people who hang around long enough to know him end up both loving him and being oddly protective. / Jordan: He has ... no companion. ... He's gonna have to trust somebody. / Fregia: In some respects, he became what he loathed about his father. / Zinke: Tiger Woods never got wet and sandy. / Narration: Tiger hated that his dad cheated on his mom and cried to his high school girlfriend about it. / Grohman (narration): worried that Tiger didn't have friends his own age until high school. His friends were Earl and Earl's old military buddies.
sources.context: Long-form reported feature (about 18 months), published ten years after Earl's death and after the scandal, so it builds a hindsight narrative. Woods did not participate. Many motive claims come from unnamed friends or SEALs; Brown's 'two paths' account is second-hand recall. 'Impersonation' and the '30 seconds' line are Thompson's narration, not testimony. Fregia was the first director of the Tiger Woods Foundation. Also establishes the birth date (31st birthday on 2006-12-30, so born 1975-12-30) and that Tiger grew up an only child of the marriage with few friends his age (per Navy course pro Joe Grohman).

sources.title: Exclusive: Tiger Woods discusses golf future in first in-depth interview since car accident (original)

claims.claim: In his 2010-02-19 statement Woods explained the affairs in his own words: 'I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply', 'I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled.'
claims.inference: His own account links achievement to exemption: a lifetime of earned results bought a private reward and a suspension of rules. 'Convinced myself' is self-deception language. This supports a worth-through-achievement reading (Type 3's self-deceptive image) more than appetite for intensity as such.
claims.alternative: A scripted statement shaped by advisers, therapists and sponsors, with therapy vocabulary; entitlement after fame is common to many celebrities regardless of type. An 8 reading treats the same passage as lust plus rule-defiance. Self-report establishes what he said, not the complete motive.

claims.claim: The same statement reframed his worth from results to character and asked for restored belief: 'it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome. Achievements on the golf course are only part of setting an example', apologized to families who 'used to point to me as a role model', to 'business partners', and closed: 'I ask you to find room in your hearts to one day believe in me again.'
claims.inference: The repair he sought was in how he was seen: role model, belief, partners. Speaking of image restoration this directly fits a 3's concern with being regarded as valuable.
claims.alternative: Sponsors (Accenture, Gillette, AT&T had dropped or paused him) and an image-based fortune gave commercial reasons to ask for belief whatever his type; crisis PR norms dictate such language.

claims.claim: On 2009-12-02 Woods called privacy 'an important and deep principle' and wrote that 'Personal sins should not require press releases and problems within a family shouldn't have to mean public confessions'; 79 days later he gave a televised confession (2010-02-19).
claims.inference: Observable reversal: privacy was the first defense, then a managed public confession once the image cost grew. Pattern of protecting the public picture first and disclosing on his own terms.
claims.alternative: The reversal can be explained by escalating sponsor pressure, the PGA Tour's interests and advice from crisis managers, not by personality. Strong privacy preference also fits Type 5.

claims.claim: In 2007, after the National Enquirer obtained photos of Woods with another woman, Woods agreed to a Men's Fitness cover and 12-page story 'about his diet, workout regimen and marriage' and the photos were not published. Reported by the NY Post and WSJ in 2009-10 (American Media denied it then) and confirmed by former AMI CEO David Pecker under oath on 2024-04-26.
claims.inference: A costly, deliberate image trade: he supplied an idealized public image (fitness and marriage) to keep a contradicting one hidden. This is the clearest observed act of protecting an image rather than confronting a threat.
claims.alternative: Brand protection was worth tens of millions in endorsements, so his agents may have driven the decision; there is no evidence of Woods' personal role or words. Pecker's testimony came 17 years later in an unrelated trial. 'Blackmail' is a reporter's word, not a finding. Sensitive: name the other woman only as reported, if at all.

claims.claim: In his 2017 book Woods wrote: 'I probably came back too early from some of the surgeries, but I was single-minded in my desire to compete and my need for competition.'
claims.inference: He names competing as a need, not just a preference, and accepts physical cost for it. Consistent with identity fused with performance.
claims.alternative: Elite athletes broadly describe competition as a need; career incentives, sponsor obligations and fear of decline explain early returns. Also fits an 8's refusal to yield to the body.

claims.claim: Before the 2008 U.S. Open, which he won in a 91-hole playoff, doctors found a torn ACL and two tibial stress fractures and advised weeks on crutches and rest. Haney recalls Woods 'is not really listening' and said 'I'm playing the U.S. Open and I'm going to win'; Williams says he asked three times whether to carry on and got 'F--- you, Stevie, I'm winning this tournament.'
claims.inference: Overriding medical advice and his own caddie to win shows willpower and an extreme priority on winning the biggest events.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest single datum for Type 8 (defiance, dominance, denial of vulnerability). Haney and Williams both later fell out with Woods. Major titles also drove his legacy and earnings. Two witnesses with independent vantage points agree, which strengthens the fact but not the motive.

claims.claim: After winning the 1997 Masters by a record 12 shots, Woods rebuilt his swing with Butch Harmon. He wrote: 'I didn't see one flaw. I saw about 10. ... by my standard, I felt I had gotten away with murder.' His reason was reliability ('I need to get the foul balls in the position where I can play and compete'), and Harmon says he refused a gradual approach: 'He wanted to do it all right now.'
claims.inference: Accepting a short-term slump after a record win to secure dominance every week. The stated goal is consistent results under pressure, not appearance. Repeated with Haney (2004) and later coaches.
claims.alternative: The perfectionist standard ('by my standard') supports Type 1; the mastery-and-control rationale supports Type 5; the impatience fits 8. A 3 reading has to treat the rebuild as investment in future winning, which is plausible but not unique.

claims.claim: In his 2022-03-09 Hall of Fame speech Woods said his parents instilled 'that nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned. If you don't go out there and put in the work ... you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. So that defined my upbringing. That defined my career.'
claims.inference: He states a rule that ties deservingness to earned results, the same logic he used in 2010 to excuse himself ('worked hard ... deserved'). The repetition across 12 years and opposite contexts (confession vs celebration) is the strongest self-report thread for a worth-through-achievement motive.
claims.alternative: This is also a Type 1 moral rule about effort and fairness, and a widely shared athlete ethic shaped by Earl's military values and racial exclusion ('twice as good to be given half a chance', S14). The line may be attributed to his mother or both parents depending on transcript.

claims.claim: Woods said in 2022: 'I made practicing so difficult, hurt so much, because I wanted to make sure that I was ready come game time. I hit thousands of balls, hands bleeding, aching, just so that I could play in a tournament.'
claims.inference: Self-imposed pain as preparation; readiness to perform is the organizing value.
claims.alternative: Fits 8 (toughness, pain tolerance), 1 (discipline) and Earl's 'train hard, fight easy' military code as learned practice rather than motive.

claims.claim: At the 2022 Open Woods criticized LIV players: 'they've turned their back on what has allowed them to get to this position' and asked 'what is the incentive to practice? What is the incentive to go out there and earn it in the dirt?' when money is guaranteed.
claims.inference: Same 'earn it' rule as C08, now applied to peers: guaranteed money without earned results is illegitimate. Worth must be earned in competition.
claims.alternative: Woods was a PGA Tour stakeholder and later a Policy Board player director, so institutional interest and loyalty (or Type 6/8 protectiveness of his side) explain the stance too.

claims.claim: LIV CEO Greg Norman said in 2022 that Woods turned down an offer of 'high nine digits'; asked about $700-800 million, Norman said 'somewhere in that neighborhood'.
claims.inference: If accurate, declining a vast guaranteed sum is a costly choice for legacy, institution and earned status over money.
claims.alternative: One-party claim by an interested rival; not opened in this research and not confirmed by Woods. Do not use as fact without opening a primary report.

claims.claim: An unnamed friend told Wright Thompson: 'the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book', and another said Woods 'was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality.'
claims.inference: Friends perceive a gap between a commercially produced public self and a private, quieter self. A split between performed image and inner self is central to the Type 3 hypothesis.
claims.alternative: Read straightforwardly, the private self described here (introverted, bookish, wanting to be left alone) is the strongest evidence for Type 5 with a commercially imposed persona. Unnamed sources; hindsight framing.

claims.claim: Asked by Notah Begay about a Halloween costume, Woods texted: 'I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods.'
claims.inference: His own joke treats 'Tiger Woods' as a costume, an awareness that the public figure is a role. Supports the image/self gap in C12.
claims.alternative: Thompson presents it as humor during a hard period. One joke cannot carry a motive claim.

claims.claim: Thompson writes that 'it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be' and that people who spend hours with him 'think he's aloof and weird', while those who know him long 'end up both loving him and being oddly protective.'
claims.inference: A reporter's synthesis of many interviews: the public persona is rehearsed and modeled on an idea of what a star should be.
claims.alternative: The same aloofness counts against a 3's usual charm and adaptiveness; it fits 5's detachment or 8's indifference to approval. Author narration, not testimony.

claims.claim: Rachel Uchitel said in HBO's 'Tiger' (2021) that Woods 'was sick of trying to hide who he was but he was so scared of the real Tiger not living up to the Tiger that everybody else thinks he is.'
claims.inference: If accurate, this names a fear of the real self failing the public image. That is close to the Type 3 core fear stated in plain language.
claims.alternative: Her interpretation, from a party with an interest in her own rehabilitation; sensitive. Do not lean on it without the independent support of C04, C12 and C13.

claims.claim: After Earl Woods died on 2006-05-03, Woods left Kansas 77 minutes after landing for the burial, visited a SEAL training facility 25 days after the burial and 15 days before the 2006 U.S. Open (where he missed his first major cut as a pro), told a SEAL his reason was 'My dad', and spent his 31st birthday (2006-12-30) skydiving with SEALs.
claims.inference: Grief channeled into his father's world and a dangerous alternative identity, at real career cost (coach objections, a missed cut). It suggests identity searching after losing his primary audience and model.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest behavior the 3 hypothesis does not explain neatly: an arena with no audience and no golf payoff. It fits an 8's appetite for intensity, a 6's identification with his father's code, or grief alone. Zinke says he 'never got wet and sandy', so the training was less immersive than legend says.

claims.claim: Woods described his own way with feeling in 2006: 'I'm kind of the one who bottles things up a little bit and moves on, tries to deal with things in my own way', before breaking down after winning the 2006 Open, saying he wished his father could have seen it.
claims.inference: Emotion is set aside for function and released only after the result. Consistent with a 3's suspended feelings in service of performance.
claims.alternative: Equally consistent with 5's compartmentalization, 8's guardedness against vulnerability, or Earl's explicit coaching not to let 'emotions get the better of you'.

claims.claim: After Charles P. Pierce's April 1997 GQ profile printed the crude jokes he told in a limo, Woods did not deny them; he said he was 'naive about the motives of certain ambitious writers' and objected to 'the attacks on my father'. Later reporters describe him as 'one of the most guarded athletes in history'.
claims.inference: An early reputational wound followed by a long era of controlled, bland media access. Protecting image by restricting access.
claims.alternative: Media guardedness is also standard advice for a young star with large endorsements, and fits 5's privacy. The source chain does not prove the GQ episode caused the change.

claims.claim: When Butch Harmon criticized his swing in 2004, Woods said Harmon 'doesn't really know what I'm working on ... and no one knows' and that friends should 'go right up to my face and say it.'
claims.inference: Secrecy about process and an insistence on private, direct criticism; public loyalty matters.
claims.alternative: The 'say it to my face' code is a classic Type 8 marker; the secrecy fits 5. A 3 reading treats it as protecting his public narrative ('I am close') during a slump, which Harmon called 'denial'.

claims.claim: Butch Harmon said in 2020 that great champions need 'a lot of prick in you' and 'just want to cut your heart out', in remarks framed by Fox Business as describing Woods' mentality.
claims.inference: A coach's view that Woods competed with a will to dominate rivals.
claims.alternative: Supports Type 8. Several quotes describe champions in general; the more specific 'win by 10' claim is snippet only.

claims.claim: At 20, in Gary Smith's 1996 'The Chosen One', Woods accepted the destiny his father proclaimed ('He's the Chosen One. He'll have the power to impact nations'), saying: 'I don't see any of this as scary or a burden. I see it as fortunate. ... This is my purpose. It will unfold.'
claims.inference: He adopted a parent-assigned identity of world-historical achievement as his own purpose early.
claims.alternative: Circumstance, not type: a child publicly framed as a chosen achiever would plausibly internalize it whatever his type. The reproduced copy is not independent; verify against SI. Earl's prophecy line is corroborated by GQ 1997.

claims.claim: Earl Woods described deliberately trying to 'break him down mentally' with distractions during Tiger's swing and said 'I pulled every nasty, dirty, ungodly trick on him', ending with 'You'll never run into another person as mentally tough as you.' Earl also said 'Let the legend grow.'
claims.inference: Earl trained imperviousness to disruption and openly cultivated the legend. Context for later toughness and image management.
claims.alternative: Earl was a self-interested mythmaker ('Let the legend grow'), so his anecdotes may be embellished. This describes the environment, not the son's motive. Do not invent a childhood wound from it.

claims.claim: At 19 (Sports Illustrated, 1995) Woods said of his father's training: 'I'd get angry sometimes. But I knew it was for the betterment of me.'
claims.inference: He framed hard treatment as self-improvement even as a teenager.
claims.alternative: Fits any type raised to value toughness; one relayed quote.

claims.claim: In 2013 Woods said that if his children played golf there would be 'no lessons ... just have fun' and that his own father had told him to 'Go play baseball'. By 2022 he described testing his son Charlie: 'if I can get into his head, that means someone else can get in his head ... That's what my dad believed in. You've got to be willing to take it.'
claims.inference: A change of mind: he came to reproduce his father's method, which shows how fully he endorses the training that formed him.
claims.alternative: Could reflect Charlie's own choices and talent rather than Woods' motive. The 2013 account of Earl steering him away from golf conflicts with biographers' accounts.

claims.claim: Woods appeared on national television (The Mike Douglas Show) at age two, in 1978, and his father later said 'Let the legend grow.'
claims.inference: He performed for an audience before he could choose to. Context for an identity built around being watched.
claims.alternative: Circumstance alone; a 5 or 8 child could have had the same upbringing. Who arranged the appearance is not documented in opened sources.

claims.claim: Woods said that as a junior 'I was not allowed in the clubhouses where all the other juniors were. The color of my skin dictated that. As I got older, that drove me even more', and that he put his shoes on in the parking lot and asked only where the first tee was and what the course record was.
claims.inference: Exclusion was converted into fuel for results; results were the answer to status denied.
claims.alternative: Racism is a real, external circumstance; this is resilience under discrimination, not proof of type. Also fits 8's defiance.

claims.claim: Days after the 1997 Masters Woods described himself as 'Cablinasian', declining to be classified simply as Black.
claims.inference: Self-definition on his own terms; refusal to let others assign identity.
claims.alternative: Primarily a statement about mixed heritage; drew criticism. Weak type evidence.

claims.claim: At the 2013 Masters Woods said he deliberately dropped 'two yards further back' to take yardage off; the drop was illegal, he was penalized two strokes, and he declined calls (e.g., Nick Faldo's) to withdraw.
claims.inference: Rules were treated pragmatically in service of competing; staying in contention outweighed a gesture of rectitude.
claims.alternative: Counts against Type 1. Withdrawal was not required by the ruling, and many players defended him (Couples).

claims.claim: After his 2017-05-29 DUI arrest Woods said 'I understand the severity of what I did ... What happened was an unexpected reaction to prescribed medications' and 'I expect more from myself, too.' Toxicology found five drugs including painkillers, sleep medication and THC; in August he said 'it was a mistake to do this without medical assistance', and he pleaded guilty to reckless driving through a diversion program.
claims.inference: Self-managed medication during severe back pain; public framing shifted as facts emerged. 'I expect more from myself' is self-standard language.
claims.alternative: Sensitive medical/legal matter. Chronic pain and surgery are the main circumstantial explanation; this is not type evidence and must not be framed as character diagnosis.

claims.claim: After winning the 2019 Masters, his 15th major, Woods said he had 'serious doubts ... I could barely walk' after 2017 and that he wanted his children 'to see their Pops win, just like my Pops saw me win here', adding 'I wasn't going to let that happen to them twice'.
claims.inference: Winning in front of the people who matter to him; the win completes a generational picture.
claims.alternative: Ordinary parental pride; also fits 2/6 belonging motives. Not a discriminator alone.

claims.claim: In November 2021, after the 2021-02-23 crash, Woods said a full return was off ('never full time, ever again—but pick and choose'), that 'I don't have to compete and play against the best players in the world to have a great life', and that he would not climb 'Mount Everest' again 'and that's okay'.
claims.inference: A stated loosening of identity from competition after near-amputation.
claims.alternative: He nonetheless kept attempting returns (2022-2024 majors, TGL, surgeries in 2024-2025), so behavior partly contradicts the statement; physical limits and business roles explain much.

claims.claim: On 2021-02-23 Woods crashed near Rancho Palos Verdes; the LA County Sheriff said the primary cause was unsafe speed (84-87 mph in a 45 zone). No impairment evidence was found and no citation was issued; Woods said he was 'grateful for all the help I received.'
claims.inference: His public reply stressed gratitude and recovery, not the speed finding.
claims.alternative: An accident under investigation that found no impairment; no type inference should rest on it.

claims.claim: Erica Herman, his girlfriend from about 2017 to 2022, alleged in 2022-2023 filings that a Woods trust broke a tenancy agreement and sought to void an NDA; a Florida judge ruled in May 2023 that she must arbitrate, and in November 2023 she dropped the case and stated she 'was never a victim of sexual harassment or sexual abuse at the hands of Tiger Woods.' Woods spoke only through counsel.
claims.inference: Pattern of confidentiality and counsel-led response rather than personal public statement.
claims.alternative: Allegations were never adjudicated on the merits and were disavowed; sensitive. Likely best omitted or stated neutrally in one line.

claims.claim: On 2026-03-27 Woods was arrested on suspicion of DUI after a rollover crash on Jupiter Island, Florida (no injuries; breath test negative; refused a urine test; deputies reported two hydrocodone pills in his pocket). He entered treatment abroad, missed every 2026 major, declined the 2027 Ryder Cup captaincy, and on 2026-09-02 took a plea deal on reduced charges (reported as reckless driving, second offense) with a five-year license suspension. As of 2026-10-04 he has not returned to competition.
claims.inference: A second medication-related driving arrest nine years after 2017, during chronic pain after a seventh back surgery. It tests the career-long pattern of controlled statements and privacy requests.
claims.alternative: Medical and legal facts, not type evidence; pain management and dependence are circumstantial explanations. Plea type conflicts between outlets (no contest vs guilty).
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods returns to competition, makes a substantive public statement about his treatment, faces any further legal matter, or if any outlet corrects the plea terms; also when a new PGA Tour or Ryder Cup role is announced.

claims.claim: Woods' statements in 2025-2026 repeatedly pair disclosure with a privacy request (mother's death 2025-02-04, relationship with Vanessa Trump 2025-03-23, treatment statement 2026-03-31), and his first public appearance after the arrest, on 2026-06-23 as chair of the PGA Tour Future Competition Committee, was a prepared statement with no questions.
claims.inference: A stable, decades-long pattern of controlled disclosure on his own terms, from 2009 to 2026.
claims.alternative: Privacy requests are standard for public figures; legal counsel would advise no questions during a pending case. Fits 5 as well as 3.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check when Woods next gives an unscripted interview or press conference, or if his role on the PGA Tour committee or board changes.

claims.claim: Woods credited his mother: 'without her none of my personal achievements would have been possible' (2025) and 'My Mom doesn't get enough credit. They all thought that it was me and Dad on the road ... but Mom was at home' (2024).
claims.inference: He corrects the Earl-centred legend of his formation himself.
claims.alternative: Ordinary filial tribute in a memorial context; useful mainly to avoid an Earl-only origin story.

claims.claim: In 1996 Woods said he liked Buddhism because 'It's based on discipline and respect and personal responsibility'; in 2010 he said Buddhism 'teaches that a craving for things outside ourselves causes an unhappy and pointless search for security' and 'to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint. Obviously, I lost track of what I was taught.'
claims.inference: His own diagnosis in 2010 is craving for external things and impulse, not image. That cuts somewhat toward the 8 (lust/impulse) or 7 readings.
claims.alternative: The vocabulary is borrowed from Buddhism and therapy. A 3 reading interprets 'things outside ourselves' as external validation, which the text does not specify.

claims.claim: Steve Williams wrote that Woods would 'flippantly toss a club in the general direction of the bag' and had a 'habit of spitting at the hole if he missed a putt', and demanded in 2010 that he show 'the game of golf — more respect'; Woods' own 2010 statement said 'I need to make my behavior more respectful of the game.'
claims.inference: On-course temper was visible and recognized by Woods himself. Image management was not total.
claims.alternative: Counter to a pure 3 reading (a 3 usually polishes visible conduct); fits 8 or 1 anger. Williams has animus and book incentives, but Woods' own line corroborates the substance.

claims.claim: In his first interviews after the scandal (2010-03-21) Woods said 'I was living a life of a lie' (other copies: 'living a lie') and spoke of 'stripping away denial and rationalization' to reach 'the truth of who you really are', and said it would be nice to hear 'a couple claps here and there'.
claims.inference: His own framing of the scandal centers on a false life and an unknown true self, and he wants the crowd's approval back.
claims.alternative: Therapy vocabulary from inpatient treatment; wording varies between copies.

claims.claim: Woods said in 2024 that his daughter Sam has 'a negative connotation to the game, because when she was growing up, golf took Daddy away from her.'
claims.inference: Names a family cost of his career.
claims.alternative: Ordinary travel cost of a touring athlete.

claims.claim: After Rory McIlroy's 2024 U.S. Open loss Woods said 'We all lose' and 'I still want the last putt', and McIlroy said Woods 'has been nothing but incredible to me'.
claims.inference: Late-career mentor warmth alongside an undiminished wish for the decisive moment.
claims.alternative: Mentoring fits many types; the change may be life stage.

claims.claim: Existing public typings of Woods found online assign Type 3 (Upbuild: 3w4; forum users: 3) without cited evidence; no Enneagram Institute listing or evidence-based alternative typing was found.
claims.inference: Prior hypothesis only; must not be counted as evidence.
claims.alternative: Low-quality consensus can be anchored on fame and ambition alone, which the standard warns against.

claims.claim: Hank Haney said by 2010 that Woods 'wanted to be a Navy SEAL. For sure that was on his list'; Woods' agent called that a twisting of his 'high respect for the military'. An unnamed friend told Thompson 'The goal was to make it through BUD/S ... It had nothing to do with golf', while former SEAL Ryan Zinke said he 'never got wet and sandy'.
claims.inference: At his peak, he seriously pursued an identity outside golf tied to his father.
claims.alternative: Contested by his camp; sources have incentives (Haney's book) or are anonymous. Supports the unexplained-behavior column rather than any type.

claims.claim: Michael Jordan told Thompson that Woods has '... no companion' and is 'gonna have to trust somebody'; Paul Fregia said 'In some respects, he became what he loathed about his father.'
claims.inference: Friends describe isolation and low trust, and a repetition of his father's infidelity (Thompson reports Tiger cried as a teen about Earl cheating on his mother).
claims.alternative: Friend's speculation and a former employee's view. Low trust fits 5, 6 and 8 as much as 3. Sensitive family material.

claims.claim: Nike's 2013 ad after Woods regained world No. 1 carried the tagline 'Winning takes care of everything'; Nike said it reflected Woods' consistent sentiment.
claims.inference: A sponsor publicly framed winning as restoring standing after the scandal.
claims.alternative: This is Nike's copy, not a verified Woods quote. Do not attribute it to him.

claims.claim: Woods said the family took a second mortgage at 14 1/2 so he could play the AJGA tour, and that the first thing he did with his first deal was pay it off.
claims.inference: Loyalty and repayment to family; achievement as provision.
claims.alternative: Fits many types; mainly a humanizing detail.

claims.claim: In his 2017 book Woods wrote of his ex-wife: 'My dishonesty and selfishness caused her intense pain. My regret will last a lifetime.'
claims.inference: Sustained ownership of the betrayal seven years later.
claims.alternative: Curated memoir voice.

claims.claim: Biographers Jeff Benedict and Armen Keteyian (2018) framed their book around the question 'Who is Tiger Woods?' and said Woods' representatives imposed conditions they would not accept for cooperation.
claims.inference: Even long-form biographers found the person hard to locate behind the managed figure.
claims.alternative: Unauthorized biography with commercial and adversarial incentives; their characterizations of Earl and of Tiger's gratitude are not used here.

claims.claim: Biographical facts for metadata: Woods was born 1975-12-30 (his 31st birthday was 2006-12-30); he has 82 PGA Tour wins (tied for the record) and 15 major championships, the 15th at the 2019 Masters; his father Earl died 2006-05-03 and his mother Kultida died 2025-02-04; his children are Sam and Charlie.
claims.inference: Factual metadata.
claims.alternative: Birthplace (Cypress, California) is widely reported but not in an opened source here; omit or source it. Record counts should be rechecked if he wins again.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check win totals if Woods records another PGA Tour or major win.

type_hypothesis.against: Several strong observations resist a Type 3 reading. (1) Peers and reporters find him aloof, cold and uninterested in being liked by most people (C14, C44), and he let on-course temper, club-tossing and spitting damage his image for years (C38). A 3 usually polishes visible conduct and charms. (2) Friends describe the private Woods as a natural introvert who wants to be left alone with a book (C12), which reads naturally as a Type 5 core behind a commercially imposed persona. (3) His defiance and will to dominate (playing the 2008 U.S. Open on a broken leg against doctors' advice and telling his caddie 'F--- you, Stevie', C06; Harmon's 'prick' mentality, C20; 'say it to my face', C19) and his appetite and impulse in 2009 (C01, C37) fit Type 8, whose passion is lust; his own 2010 Buddhist diagnosis names craving and impulse, not image (C37). (4) After 2021 he repeatedly risked public failure in diminished comebacks (C31), the exposure a 3 is said to avoid. (5) Much of his image control has a commercial explanation: endorsements dwarfed prize money, and his agents may have made the 2007 Enquirer deal (C04). (6) The moral rules ('you don't deserve it', 'I expect more from myself', 'core values', C08, C29, C01) and swing perfectionism ('by my standard', C07) give a Type 1 reading some support. (7) Being proclaimed 'the Chosen One' and on national TV at two (C21, C25) is circumstance that could produce a performance-centred identity in any type.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 8 is the strongest alternative. It explains overriding his doctors and caddie to win the 2008 U.S. Open on a torn ACL and two stress fractures (C06), the intimidation and desire to crush rivals that coaches describe (C20), his self-imposed painful practice (C09), the face-to-face loyalty code and secrecy toward his old coach (C19), the denial of vulnerability ('bottles things up', C17), the excess and impulse of the 2009 affairs that he himself framed as craving (C01, C37), the risk-seeking SEAL training (C16, C43), visible temper on the course (C38), and fierce protection of his family and institution (C03, C10). Type 5 is a serious second alternative: the introvert friends describe (C12), lifelong privacy and secrecy about his process (C03, C19, C35), compartmentalization (C17), an adult and military childhood world with few peers (C17 source S17), and low trust (C44). Type 1 is a weaker third: standards, 'core values', 'I expect more from myself' and swing perfectionism (C07, C08, C29), but it fails against 'I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply' (C01) and the pragmatic 2013 drop (C28).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when the public picture and the private reality diverge. Across decades Woods' characteristic move is to manage the picture, not to own the appetite openly (the 8 pattern) or to withdraw from public exposure (the 5 pattern). In 2007 he supplied an idealized fitness-and-marriage cover story so contradicting photos stayed buried (C04, Pecker's sworn 2024 testimony). In 2009 he invoked privacy as principle, then staged a confession that apologized to business partners and to parents who used him as a role model and asked the public to 'believe in me again' (C02, C03). His private self-justification was that earned results bought exemption: 'worked hard my entire life and deserved ... I felt I was entitled' (C01). The same earned-equals-deserving rule recurs unprompted in opposite contexts across 26 years: 'This is my purpose' at 20 (C21), the 2010 confession (C01), 'need for competition' in 2017 (C05), 'you don't deserve it ... You need to earn it ... That defined my career' in 2022 (C08), and 'earn it in the dirt' against LIV in 2022 (C10). Friends describe the public figure as a role he performs ('a golfer known as Tiger Woods', 'impersonation', the real one 'isn't that marketable', C12-C14) and a partner says he feared 'the real Tiger not living up to the Tiger that everybody else thinks he is' (C15). An 8 is not usually troubled by a gap between persona and self and does not ask to be believed in again. A 5 minimizes appetite and public spectacle rather than seeking the largest stage. Commercial incentive explains brand protection, but not the private 2010 self-justification or the 2022 moral rule about deserving. The 8 explanation must still answer C06 and C20, so confidence stays medium.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The Navy SEAL pursuit at his peak and in the months after his father's death (C16, C43): a dangerous, audience-less identity tied to Earl that cost him at the 2006 U.S. Open and has no golf payoff. The bookish homebody friends describe beside the Las Vegas nights. Coldness toward people whose admiration a 3 would court (C14), and on-course temper he let damage his image (C38). His late-career warmth as a mentor and his tears at the Hall of Fame (C41, S12) beside lifelong guardedness. The shift from 'no lessons' to Earl-style mental tests with his son (C24). Becoming, in a former foundation director's words, what he loathed in his father (C44). The 2017 and 2026 medication-related driving arrests (C29, C34) are best explained by chronic pain after seven back surgeries and are not type evidence. The Norman offer (C11), if true, shows money ranked below status and institution, which fits several types.
